k-1.x_notes: Strengths: the header and footer follow the organizer's format, there is no Name field, and the pages are uncluttered. Each of the seven problems has one action stated in a single sentence (color the star, cross out the counters to take, circle 1st/2nd), so pre-readers can act on it. The counter pictures are large. The sequence works: winning piles 1-6, then the winning move for piles 4-11, then losing piles 1-15 on a tower chart that shows the multiples-of-3 pattern, then a 20-counter match against a grown-up with stars for repeated games. After that come rule changes ({1,2,3}, then {1,3} with its odd/even pattern) and two-row games where copying the partner wins, including the non-copy case 2|3. All answers check out. Weaknesses: 'always win' is never defined for K-1. There is no explicit task about answering every reply. 'Tell how you win' in P7 has no recording space, though an oral answer is fine at this age.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: nine problems with more reasoning variety. P3 introduces the 'trap' idea (the outline's K-1 emphasis). P4 is a branching picture: for each partner move, what do you take next? It makes 'answer every reply' concrete. P5 asks which turn of a recorded 8-counter game was the mistake; the unique answer, row 3, is correct. P6 has the child choose who goes first against the adult with 9 counters. P7 extends traps past 12 and 20, P8 changes the rule to {1,2,3}, and P9 has two-pile games including the non-mirror second-player win 4|1. All answers check out. Weaknesses: every page has a Name field (which the organizer banned), the header is in the wrong format, and there is no footer. Definitions and rules sit in boxes, including a mid-packet trap definition. P1 and P2 are thin one-glance warm-ups. P5 and the trap definition are wordy and abstract for kindergartners and need an adult to interpret, which matters if the parent volunteer runs this table.
k-1.reason: Both packets are correct and fill the time. Y has a couple of richer reasoning items (the reply tree and the game-record mistake). X's pages are clearer for non-readers, every problem is substantial, the format is right, and the rule changes are well chosen, so X will run more smoothly at a K-1 table.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: correct format. The ramp starts at {1,2} piles 1-20, then asks first/second and the opening move for 24/29/31/45 with a 'why it wins no matter what' explanation. Next comes {1,3,4} piles 1-20 (losing at 2,7,9,14,16). P4 has five named claims to test: take 4 from 5, second wins at 7, first wins at 9, take 1 from 10, and 'taking 4 is always best'. These are well chosen; Mia, Zoe and Ana are wrong and Leo and Sam are right. P5 asks about 30/50/100 to force the period-7 idea. P6 has two-row {1,2} pictures including the non-mirror second-player wins 3|6 and 1|4. P7 compares four rules at 35 (first, first, second, second). All answers verified. Weaknesses: the {1,2} start may go quickly for third graders. P7 needs four new patterns worked out with no tables provided and is closer to 4-5 content.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: a coherent focus on {1,3,4}, matching the band emphasis, with clear definitions of winning and losing piles. P1 is concrete (play from 6 several times). P2 fills in W/L for 1-20. P3 is the greedy claim and P4 is the copycat claim at 8, both false; these test strategies against every reply. P5 is a lovely game-record table in which turns 2 and 3 are the mistakes. P6 asks for a full plan for the second player at 14. P7 covers big piles 23/28/33/50/100. P8 is {1,3,5} with a description of all losing piles. P9 has two {1,3,4} piles, including 6|4 (a second-player win from two winning piles). All verified. Weaknesses: Name field on every page, wrong header, no footer. P5's literal wording also qualifies turns 4 and 6 (a different winning move existed), so it is slightly ambiguous. P9 needs heavy case analysis for third graders.
grades-2-3.reason: Both are substantial, correct, and well sequenced. Y concentrates more on testing strategies against every reply, while X has the better format, a gentler entry, and a more level-appropriate two-pile problem. I would be equally happy taking either.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: correct format and plain-language rules. The problems start concrete and build: {1,2} and {1,2,3} tables, then exact strategies for 100 counters, then {1,3,4} to 30 with 100/1000 and why the pattern continues forever. P5 compares {1,3,5} (even piles), {1,4} (0 and 2 mod 5) and {1,4,5} (0 and 2 mod 8). P6 adds one number to {1,2}: 4, 5 and 7 leave the multiples of 3 unchanged, while 6 gives 0 and 3 mod 7, which leads to the insight about adding a multiple of 3. P7 is an excellent inverse design problem: {1,2,3,4} works, {1,2,3,5} works, evens with 2 allowed is impossible, and 'only 3' is impossible for a finite rule. P8 uses grids to make two-pile games visible, and grid (b) quietly exposes the Grundy-value structure. All answers verified. Weaknesses: P1(a) is trivial for this band. There are several similar classification tables. P8(b) is a large amount of computation. It never names Sprague-Grundy values.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: ambitious and mathematically correct. P3 is the greedy player against a careful opponent; the greedy player wins only from 1, 3, 4, 6 and 11, which is very nice. P4 asks for every rule containing 1 with the same losing piles as {1,3,5} (all odd move sets). P5 is {1,2,m} (m a multiple of 3 changes the pattern). P6 is {1,6,9}, where the pattern settles into a period-5 cycle from pile 10. P7 asks for the pigeonhole proof of eventual periodicity. P8 to P10 define mex values and use them on two piles: 6|4 and 12|5 lose, 5|1 and 11|3 win. Weaknesses: it reads like an undergraduate problem set, with set notation, a variable m, 'every finite set', and a mex definition. There is no concrete entry and no diagrams. Several problems (P5 for all m, P7 for every finite set, P10) are open-ended proofs that 9- and 10-year-olds are unlikely to manage on their own. There is a Name field, the header and footer are wrong, and a second rule box sits mid-packet.
grades-4-5.reason: X develops the band's core ideas (patterns, why they repeat, how changing the rule changes them) through concrete tables, grids and a strong design problem pitched at 4th-5th graders. Y's content is deeper but abstract and proof-heavy from the start, so children would stall without constant adult help.

overall.reason: Both packets are mathematically sound throughout. X is clearly better pitched for grades 4-5, slightly clearer for K-1, and even with Y for grades 2-3. X also follows the organizer's page format, while Y has Name fields and the wrong header and footer on every page.
